questions.problem:
The velocity, in $\text{m/s}$, of a subatomic particle is modeled using the function $v(t)=2{csc}^{2}⁡(t)$ for $\pi <t<2\pi .$

Current part:

Find the velocity of the particle at $t=\frac{7\pi }{6}.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $v(\frac{7\pi }{6})\,=\,$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $\text{m/s}$
questions.worked_solution:
Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13942110/assets/dbf36192ac332dc49ed75278838e989a37ac7d888311be1b8b059a7b59667aa6.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{7\pi }{6}$ corresponds to the point $(-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},-\frac{1}{2}).$

Since the sine of the angle corresponds to the $y$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})=-\frac{1}{2}.$

Therefore, using the fact that $\operatorname{csc}⁡\theta =\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta },$ we have

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})=\frac{1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})}=\frac{1}{(-\frac{1}{2})}=-2.
$$

Finally, evaluating $v(t)$ at $t=\frac{7\pi }{6}$ we have

$$
2{csc}^{2}⁡(\frac{7\pi }{6})=2{(-2)}^{2}=8.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Computing the Limit of a Cosecant Function
questions.problem:
The velocity, in $\text{m/s}$, of a subatomic particle is modeled using the function $v(t)=2{csc}^{2}⁡(t)$ for $\pi <t<2\pi .$

Earlier part 1:

Find the velocity of the particle at $t=\frac{7\pi }{6}.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $v(\frac{7\pi }{6})\,=\,$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        $8$                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $\text{m/s}$

Current part:

${lim}_{t\to 2{\pi }^{-}}v(t)\,=\,$

                            
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Substituting $t=2\pi $ directly into the limit, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2{\pi }^{-}}v(t) & ={lim}_{t\to 2{\pi }^{-}}2{csc}^{2}⁡(t) \\  & =2{csc}^{2}⁡(2\pi ) \\  & =2\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡(2\pi )} \\  & =\frac{2}{{(0)}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{2}{0},\end{aligned}
$$

which is undefined.

Therefore, to find the limit, let's sketch the graph of $y=\operatorname{csc}⁡t.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13942110/assets/361e8bf3b622fc2e73be712dae4ec5d189bd15eecbd33c9295db7365bcf71943.png)

As $t$ approaches $2\pi $ from the left, the values of $y=\operatorname{csc}⁡t$ are negative and decrease without bound. 

Therefore

$$
{lim}_{t\to 2{\pi }^{-}}\operatorname{csc}⁡t=-\infty 
$$

Applying the product and power rules, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{t\to 2{\pi }^{-}}2{csc}^{2}⁡(2\pi ) & ={lim}_{t\to 2{\pi }^{-}}2\cdot {lim}_{t\to 2{\pi }^{-}}{csc}^{2}⁡(t) \\  & =2\cdot {({lim}_{t\to 2{\pi }^{-}}\operatorname{csc}⁡(t))}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying by the positive constant $2$ does not change the sign of the limit, so we have

$$
2\cdot {({lim}_{t\to 2{\pi }^{-}}\operatorname{csc}⁡(t))}^{2}=\infty .
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Differentiating a Power of a Trigonometric Function Using the Chain Rule
questions.problem:
The velocity, in $\text{m/s}$, of a subatomic particle is modeled using the function $v(t)=2{csc}^{2}⁡(t)$ for $\pi <t<2\pi .$

Earlier part 1:

Find the velocity of the particle at $t=\frac{7\pi }{6}.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $v(\frac{7\pi }{6})\,=\,$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        $8$                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $\text{m/s}$

Earlier part 2:

${lim}_{t\to 2{\pi }^{-}}v(t)\,=\,$

                            
                                    
                            
                                        $\infty$

Current part:

The acceleration $a(t)$ of the particle is given by the derivative of the velocity with respect to time. Find the function $a(t).$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $a(t)=$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $\cdot \operatorname{cot}⁡t$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write

$$
v(t)=2{csc}^{2}⁡(t).
$$

Now, we see that $v(t)$ can be expressed as the composite function

$$
v=2{u}^{2},\,u=\operatorname{csc}⁡t.
$$

Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}=4u,\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t}=-\operatorname{csc}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t.
$$

We now apply the chain rule and get

$$
\begin{aligned}a(t) & ={v}^{′}(t) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}t} \\  & =4u\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t) \\  & =(4\operatorname{csc}⁡t)\cdot (-\operatorname{csc}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t) \\  & =-4{csc}^{2}⁡t\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Current part:

Another particle has a velocity function given by ${v}_{2}(t)=t\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2}).$ Evaluate the velocity of this particle at $t=\frac{16\pi }{3}.$

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        ${v}_{2}(\frac{16\pi }{3})\,=\,$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $\text{m/s}$
questions.worked_solution:
Evaluating the function ${v}_{2}(t)$ at $t=\frac{16\pi }{3}$, we get

$$
{v}_{2}(\frac{16\pi }{3})=(\frac{16\pi }{3})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{8\pi }{3})
$$

First, we find an angle that's coterminal with $\frac{8\pi }{3}$ that lies in the range $[0,2\pi ).$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{8\pi }{3}-2\pi  & =\frac{2\pi }{3}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{8\pi }{3})=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3}).$

Let's remind ourselves of the special trigonometric ratios, as given by the unit circle.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/13942110/assets/dbf36192ac332dc49ed75278838e989a37ac7d888311be1b8b059a7b59667aa6.png)

From the unit circle, we see that the angle $\frac{2\pi }{3}$ corresponds to the point $(-\frac{1}{2},\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}).$

Since the cosine of the angle corresponds to the $x$-coordinate, we have $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{2\pi }{3})=-\frac{1}{2}.$

Therefore, $\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{8\pi }{3})=-\frac{1}{2}.$

Finally, 

$$
{v}_{2}(\frac{16\pi }{3})=(\frac{16\pi }{3})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{8\pi }{3})=-\frac{8\pi }{3}.
$$

Earlier part 5:

Another particle has a velocity function given by ${v}_{2}(t)=t\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2}).$ Evaluate the velocity of this particle at $t=\frac{16\pi }{3}.$

                                        $-\frac{8\pi}{3}$                
                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        $\text{m/s}$

Earlier part 6:

Find ${lim}_{t\to 5\pi /2}{v}_{2}(t)\,=\,$

                            
                                    
                            
                                        $-\frac{5\pi\sqrt{2}}{4}$

Current part:

Find the acceleration function ${a}_{2}(t)$ of the second particle.

                            
                                    
                                        
                                            

                                                

                                        
                                        
                                        

                                    
                                
                                    
                                        
                                        ${a}_{2}(t)\,=\,$

                                    
                                
                                    
                            
                                        {{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
In part 3, we saw that the derivative of a particle's velocity with respect to time gives its acceleration.

To differentiate ${v}_{2}(t),$ we require the product rule. Let $g(t)=t$ and $h(t)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2}).$ Then

$$
{g}^{′}(t)=1,\,{h}^{′}(t)=-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2}).
$$

We used the chain rule to calculate ${h}^{′}(t).$

Now, applying the product rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{2}(t) & ={v}_{2}^{′}(t) \\  & ={g}^{′}(t)\cdot h(t)+g(t)\cdot {h}^{′}(t) \\  & =(1)(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2}))+(t)(-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2})) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{t}{2})-\frac{1}{2}t\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{t}{2}).\end{aligned}
$$
